items.title: Your kidneys filter 180 litres of blood plasma every day
items.claim: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Together they filter 125 ml of plasma per minute — 180 litres per day. Your final urine output is 1 to 2 litres. The kidneys reabsorb 99% of what they filter.
items.prompt: Why filter so much only to put it back?

options.text: Bulk filtration is the only way to expose all blood-borne solutes to selective reabsorption; the kidney keeps what's needed (glucose, salts, amino acids, water) and lets the rest go — fine selectivity requires high throughput
The body has extra water to spare

items.reveal:
The glomerulus is a knot of capillaries inside a Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure forces plasma (minus proteins and cells) through a selective barrier into the nephron tubule.

Flow rates: glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ~120-125 ml/min in healthy adults. Total renal blood flow ~1.2 L/min — about 20-25% of cardiac output. The kidneys take a major share of the circulation for their mass.

The filtrate then passes through the tubules. Proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, most salts, water. Loop of Henle sets up an osmotic gradient. Distal tubule fine-tunes. Collecting duct adjusts water under ADH (antidiuretic hormone).

Result: 180 L filtered, 178.5 L returned to blood, 1.5 L excreted as urine.

GFR drops with age (~1% per year after 40), kidney disease, dehydration. Maintaining it is why drinking water matters — and why drugs that affect kidney function require careful monitoring.
items.why: Filtration that throws everything out and re-claims most of it sounds wasteful. It's the simplest design that ensures any potentially harmful blood-borne molecule eventually leaves the body.

items.title: Neurons don't 'fire harder' — they fire faster or not at all
items.claim: A neuron's action potential is all-or-nothing. The size of every action potential in a given neuron is essentially identical. Strong stimuli don't make bigger spikes — they make more spikes per second.

options.text: By the amplitude of each action potential
By the FREQUENCY of action potentials (and by the pattern of which neurons fire and when) — the rate code is the simplest model, but timing and synchrony also carry information
By the colour of the signal
By the chemical identity of each spike

items.reveal_title: Edgar Adrian and the discovery of the rate code
items.reveal:
Edgar Adrian (Nobel 1932) recorded from single sensory neurons in frogs and found: stretch a muscle and the neuron fires more spikes per second. Spike amplitude didn't change. The signal was the frequency.

Action potentials are regenerative — voltage-gated sodium channels self-amplify any membrane depolarisation past threshold into a stereotyped spike, then sodium channels inactivate and potassium channels repolarise. Sub-threshold stimuli produce no spike at all; supra-threshold stimuli produce one spike, of fixed size.

The brain reads intensity from spike rate, fine timing from spike intervals, and 'identity' from which neurons fired. Some neural systems (auditory, visual) encode information in spike timing to within a millisecond.
items.why: Sensory intensity feels continuous. The neuron encoding it is digital — and the continuous sensation is reconstructed from spike statistics.

items.title: Octopuses change colour while being colour-blind
items.claim: Cephalopods produce sophisticated colour displays — mimicking corals, fish, sand — using chromatophore cells embedded in the skin. Their actual eyes have only one photoreceptor type. They cannot distinguish red from green.
items.prompt: How do octopuses match colour without seeing it?

options.text: They have hidden colour vision we haven't found
Their SKIN contains opsin proteins — the same light-sensitive receptors used in eyes — likely giving the surface itself wavelength-sensitivity that the eyes lack
Other octopuses signal the colour to them

items.reveal_title: Distributed colour vision via opsin-expressing skin
items.reveal:
Cephalopod skin expresses several genes (including r-opsin and rhodopsin-like proteins) usually found in eyes. Ramirez and Oakley (2015) showed Octopus bimaculoides skin responds to specific wavelengths.

The hypothesis: the chromatic information bypasses the brain entirely. The skin senses ambient colour and adjusts the chromatophore display locally without needing centralised colour vision.

It's also possible they exploit the chromatic aberration of their unusual U-shaped pupils to extract colour information from a single photoreceptor type — Stubbs and Stubbs (2016) — but the experimental support is mixed. Either way, cephalopod colour matching is a fascinating biological riddle.
items.why: Vision is assumed to happen in eyes and brains. In cephalopods it may happen distributed across the body.
